quote: Have among yourselves the same attitude that is also yours in Christ Jesus.
firstReading: Ezekiel answers those who accuse God’s way of being unfair. The Lord judges each person according to the course he or she freely embraces. When the wicked turn from wrongdoing and practice what is right, they preserve life; when the just abandon righteousness for iniquity, they incur death. God’s judgment exposes human responsibility while opening a real path of conversion.
secondReading: Paul appeals to the Philippians for unity rooted in Christ. They are to act from love, humility, and concern for one another rather than rivalry or vanity. Their pattern is Jesus, who accepted the condition of a servant and obediently endured death on the cross. Therefore God exalted him, so that every creature may confess Jesus Christ as Lord to the glory of the Father.
psalmSummary: Psalm 25 is a prayer of humble dependence upon the Lord. The psalmist asks God to make known his ways, teach his paths, and lead him in saving truth. Trust rests in God’s compassion and enduring mercy, which do not hold past sins against the penitent. Because the Lord is upright and gracious, he instructs sinners and guides the humble in justice.
gospelSummary: Jesus tells the chief priests and elders about two sons asked by their father to work in the vineyard. The first initially refuses but later changes his mind and goes; the second gives an outwardly willing reply but does not act. Jesus asks which son did the father’s will, and they rightly identify the first. He then applies the parable sharply: tax collectors and prostitutes, responding to John’s call to repentance, are entering God’s kingdom ahead of religious leaders who saw this response yet would not believe. The Gospel distinguishes verbal assent from obedient conversion and reveals that repentance can redirect a life toward the Father’s will.
saintReflection: Saint Vincent de Paul (Memorial): Saint Vincent de Paul (1581–1660), a French priest, became deeply attentive to the spiritual and bodily suffering of people neglected by the society around him. He founded the Congregation of the Mission to preach among the rural poor and, with Saint Louise de Marillac, helped establish the Daughters of Charity for direct service to those in need. He also worked for the formation of priests, recognizing that the Church's renewal required both sound teaching and holiness of life. His spirituality joins prayer to effective compassion: Christ encountered in worship is also to be served in the hungry, sick, and abandoned. This is the demand of Matthew 25, not simply a preference for benevolent activity. Vincent's witness calls for humility, gentleness, and persevering charity, asking whether devotion is making the faithful more attentive to suffering and more willing to respond.
dailyPrayer:
Merciful Father, teach us your paths and lead us in your truth. We confess that our lips can be ready with assent while our hearts resist the work you ask of us. Turn us from sin, from pride, and from every refusal of your grace. Give us the mind of Christ Jesus, who humbled himself in loving obedience and gave himself completely for our salvation.

Through the intercession of Saint Vincent de Paul, make us attentive to those who are hungry, sick, abandoned, and burdened in body or spirit. Purify our worship so that it bears fruit in mercy, and make our service an offering joined to the sacrifice of your Son. Strengthen priests and all the baptized in holiness, sound faith, gentleness, and steadfast charity. May we not merely speak your will, but do it, trusting that your compassion receives every repentant heart. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
The readings proclaim that God’s justice is inseparable from his merciful summons to conversion. Ezekiel rejects fatalism: the sinner is not imprisoned in sin, for turning toward what is right opens the way of life. Psalm 25 gives conversion its proper form, a humble plea that God himself teach and guide the sinner. The Gospel then makes clear that religious speech, even speech addressed to God, cannot substitute for obedience. The first son’s delayed response becomes true filial action because he repents and goes.

Philippians reveals the deepest shape of this obedience in Christ. The eternal Son does not cling to privilege but takes the form of a servant and obeys the Father unto death. Christian humility is therefore participation in the self-giving pattern of the crucified and exalted Lord. Saint Vincent de Paul’s care for those neglected in suffering belongs to this Gospel pattern: Christ is received in worship and served in those in need. Conversion bears visible fruit in mercy, while all glory returns to the Father through Jesus Christ.
exegesis:
Context: The twenty-sixth Sunday in Ordinary Time gathers its readings around conversion, obedience, and humility. Ezekiel speaks to a people tempted to question God’s justice. Their complaint assumes that divine judgment is arbitrary or that a person is bound forever by a former condition. The prophet reverses the charge: the Lord’s way is right, and each person is summoned to turn from evil and live. This is not a denial of the gravity of sin. Rather, it announces that God does not delight in a sinner’s ruin and that repentance is a real passage from death toward life. The passage calls for personal responsibility, yet it does so under the horizon of divine mercy, which continually summons the human heart back to the good.

Context: Paul gives this call its specifically Christological center. The Philippians are not simply urged to be agreeable; they are called to a communion shaped by the Lord’s own descent in love. Rivalry and self-seeking contradict the life bestowed in Christ because they place the self at the center. Humility looks to the good of others because Jesus, though truly divine, embraced servanthood. His obedience reaches the cross, where he offers himself entirely to the Father for the salvation of the world. The Father’s exaltation of the Son shows that the cross is not defeat but the revelation of divine glory. Every confession that Jesus is Lord is directed to the glory of God the Father, and it forms believers in the same obedient love.

Psalm: Psalm 25 supplies the prayer that the other readings require. Conversion cannot be reduced to a person’s isolated moral resolve. The psalmist asks the Lord to show, teach, and guide, acknowledging that God’s mercy precedes and sustains every return. The appeal that former sins not be remembered rests not on human deserving but on the goodness of God. Yet mercy does not leave the sinner unchanged. The upright Lord instructs sinners in the way and leads the humble in what is right. Humility, then, is truthful receptivity before God: it admits need, receives divine instruction, and walks in the path God gives. This prayer prevents the call to obedience from becoming self-righteousness.

Gospel: In Matthew, Jesus addresses chief priests and elders shortly after entering Jerusalem and confronting the corruption of the temple. His parable of the two sons is concise but searching. Both sons receive the father’s command; the decisive difference is not their first spoken response but whether they finally do his will. The first son’s initial refusal is grave, but he changes his mind and goes into the vineyard. The second offers the appropriate answer, yet his promise remains barren. Jesus applies the parable to the response to John the Baptist. Those publicly known as sinners believed John and accepted his call to repentance. The leaders, although they witnessed this conversion, did not allow it to bring them to faith. The kingdom is thus entered not by status or correct language alone, but by trusting repentance that bears obedience.

Saints: Saint Vincent de Paul’s witness belongs closely to this Gospel. He became attentive to people neglected in spiritual and bodily suffering, and his ministry united preaching, service, and the formation of priests. His work with Saint Louise de Marillac in establishing the Daughters of Charity expressed a conviction central to the Church’s faith: the Christ adored in worship is also to be served in the hungry, sick, and abandoned. This does not set mercy against doctrine or prayer against action. Vincent recognized that the Church’s renewal requires sound teaching and holiness of life, while the Gospel demands that love of God take concrete form in love of neighbor. His humility, gentleness, and persevering charity reflect the pattern Paul names: the mind of Christ, the servant who obeys in love.

Today: These texts examine the difference between professed faith and obedient faith. They also forbid despair. A past refusal need not be the final word when grace brings repentance; Ezekiel and the first son both witness to the possibility of a changed direction. At the same time, visible religious standing gives no immunity from the need to listen, believe, and act. The Church prays Psalm 25 because she knows that only God can teach her his ways and cleanse her memory of sin. In the Eucharistic sacrifice, believers receive the self-giving Christ and are sent to embody his humility in works of mercy. Following Saint Vincent de Paul, the faithful are called to notice those who suffer and to respond with reverence, patience, and steadfast charity. Such service is not an addition to discipleship but a fruit of conversion to the Father’s will.
